name: Chloe Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Chloe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't answer to any company, union or government, and what you say won't be linked to you. Could you start by telling me about an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the water cart at the zinc mine at Morrow's Crossing, and I fill in on the grader when they're short. The water cart is a big truck with sprayers, and I keep the dust down on the haul roads so the drivers can see. My grandfather worked underground at the old shaft here, so it's three generations now with my son Josh.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of the day for you, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is first light, when the roads are wet and shining and the dust hasn't come up yet. The hardest is summer afternoons, when you can't spray fast enough and the radio's full of drivers grumbling at you. I've got a plain phone, the one with buttons, and I like it that way. Robert, my husband, tells me I'm the last person in Morrow's Crossing without a smartphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could have told them that. All these clever people in the cities get excited about gadgets, and the rest of us still have to turn up and do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can keep going until I'm sixty-five, and Josh has a job at the mine for as long as there's ore. That's what I pray for, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep our bit of savings in the credit union, and help Robert at his mower repair shop on my days off like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, really. Like Sunday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any AI or automation at your mine now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've talked about water carts that drive themselves at other mines. Here it's mostly the computers in the office. I don't go near the office if I can help it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned prayer. What part does church play for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm on the fete committee at St Aidan's and I do the flowers once a month. If anything went wrong for anyone at the mine, it's the church ladies who'd turn up with casseroles before any government did.

S0.say: I'd say I could have told them, because clever people in the cities get excited about gadgets and the rest of us still turn up and work. I'd say it plainly.
S0.think: Privately it means I can keep going to sixty-five and my son keeps his job at the mine while there's ore. That's what I pray for.
S0.do: Keeps working her shifts, saving at the credit union and helping her husband at his mower repair shop on days off. Changes nothing.
S0.quote: It's the church ladies who'd turn up with casseroles before any government did.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is calm and rooted: three generations at one mine and a church community she trusts more than government. Her scepticism of 'clever people in the cities' sets up who she blames later. She avoids technology entirely and is proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they should keep the jobs local and look after the families who built this town. I'd say it at the pub and at church, not online, I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me more for Josh than for me. If they bring in water carts that drive themselves, they'll bring in the rest too, and his fitter's job is only safe if they still need fitters. Me, I'm average, and I won't touch a computer, so I'm an easy one to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job as well as I can and not give them an excuse. I'd put more into the credit union account, maybe a hundred a fortnight, and stop the new kitchen we've been planning. And I'd sit Josh down and tell him to get his electrical ticket too, while the mine's still paying for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be short with Robert, which isn't fair to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch a computer. If the mine offered you a course to run the self-driving water carts, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather go back to the mower shop with Robert than sit in a box watching a screen. I know that's stubborn, but I'm fifty-eight, not twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies and the people who think a town is just a cost on a spreadsheet. Not the mine manager, he's from here. He'd just be doing what head office tells him.

S1.say: I'd say they should keep the jobs local and look after the families who built this town. I'd say it at the pub and at church, not online.
S1.think: Privately it frightens me more for my son than for me, because his fitter's job is only safe while they need fitters. I'm average and won't touch a computer, so I'm easy to drop.
S1.do: Works carefully so as not to give the mine an excuse and saves an extra hundred a fortnight. Cancels the planned new kitchen and urges her son to get an electrical licence while the mine still pays for training.
S1.feel: Anxious and short-tempered with her husband, which she knows isn't fair.
S1.quote: I'd rather go back to the mower shop with Robert than sit in a box watching a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Chloe's anxiety here is about her family line at the mine as much as her own job. She refuses retraining outright and owns the stubbornness. She blames big tech and head office rather than the local manager she knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, plain wrong, and nobody asked the people it lands on. I'd sign anything that tried to slow it down, though I wouldn't want the government handing out money to everyone forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm sixty and Josh is thirty, both out of the same mine in the same year. Robert's mower shop barely covers itself. We've got maybe three months saved, and I can't see how that stretches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That first week we'd cut everything that isn't food, power and the mortgage. I'd go into the mower shop with Robert full-time and try to make it pay, sharpening blades and servicing chainsaws. We'd offer Josh and his kids our spare rooms if they needed them, and I'd lean on the church, much as it'd shame me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick with it. I'd be awake at three in the morning, listening to Robert snore and doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want the government handing out money forever. What if that was the only help available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it and hate it. I'd tell myself it's only until the shop picks up. That's not very consistent of me, is it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to let Josh get settled somewhere else before I'm out. With two years it all lands at once, on all of us. It's the together part that scares me.

S2.say: I'd say it's plain wrong and nobody asked the people it lands on. I'd sign anything to slow it down, though I wouldn't want the government handing out money forever.
S2.think: Privately I'd be sixty and my son thirty, both out of the same mine in the same year. With three months saved and my husband's shop barely covering itself, I can't see how we'd manage.
S2.do: Cuts everything but food, power and the mortgage in the first week and works full-time in her husband's mower shop to make it pay. Offers her son's family their spare rooms and leans on the church despite the shame.
S2.feel: Sick with worry, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: Then I'd take it and hate it. I'd tell myself it's only until the shop picks up.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits Chloe through her family: she and her son would lose jobs at the same mine at once. She admits, unprompted, that she'd accept welfare she disapproves of. Family and church are her first supports, the shop her only plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that it's wrong. But I'd add that people here need to start getting ready, and the mine should keep training apprentices while it can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three. If I can hang on, I'd be close enough to sixty-five to scrape by. Josh is the one I'd lie awake over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare dollar and try to pay off the mortgage before I'm out. I'd keep pushing Josh to get his electrical ticket and maybe look at work in the city. And I'd work up the mower shop slowly so it's ready for me when the mine's done with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but it's a slower kind. I'd have time to pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost you if Josh moved to the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grandkids at Sunday lunch, mostly. Lily's six and Sam's four. I'd hate it, but I'd tell him to go if it meant a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first from the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new kitchen's already gone. Then the trip to the coast at Christmas. I'd keep the church giving, though, that's not negotiable.

S3.say: I'd say it's still wrong, but people here need to start getting ready and the mine should keep training apprentices while it can.
S3.think: Privately five years takes me to sixty-three, close enough to sixty-five to scrape by if I hang on. My son is the one I'd lie awake over.
S3.do: Saves every spare dollar to pay off the mortgage before she leaves the mine and keeps pressing her son to qualify as an electrician and consider city work. Slowly builds up the mower shop as her next job.
S3.feel: Still anxious, but a slower kind with time to pray on it.
S3.quote: I'd keep the church giving, though, that's not negotiable.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Chloe a near-path to her pension, but her worry stays fixed on her son and grandchildren. She'd tell her son to move away even though it costs her Sunday lunches. Her priorities are clear in what she would never cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and the young ones should take it. Learn a trade that still needs hands, that's what I'd tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and done. I'd be at the mower shop with Robert, maybe, or just doing the church flowers. It's Josh and the grandkids I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-five as planned and keep saving at the credit union. I'd keep at Josh to get a second trade. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but for them, not me. Ten years feels like a long time when you're my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What trade would you want for the grandkids, if robots can do hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd have said plumbing or nursing, but if robots can do all of it, I can't tell you. Maybe I'd tell them to stay close to family, that's the one thing a robot can't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that worries you about the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Morrow's Crossing without the mine is just a road through. St Aidan's would lose half its people. I'd want somebody to fight for it, I just don't know who.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and the young ones should take it. Learn a trade that still needs hands is what I'd tell them.
S4.think: Privately I'd be sixty-eight and done, at the mower shop or doing the church flowers. My son and grandchildren are who I'd think about.
S4.do: Works to sixty-five as planned and keeps saving at the credit union. Keeps urging her son to get a second trade.
S4.feel: Uneasy for her family rather than herself.
S4.quote: Maybe I'd tell them to stay close to family, that's the one thing a robot can't be.
S4.fieldNote: Age protects Chloe in this version, so her worry is for her son, grandchildren and church. She admits she can't name a safe trade if robots do hands-on work. Her final answer is family, which fits everything else she says.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, with me and Josh going out the same door. What would help is the mine keeping on apprentices and older workers till the last possible day, and people round here sticking together. I don't want a handout, I want my son to have work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dust. Somebody has to keep it down for the people still there. If the robots don't mind dust, I suppose that's one thing they'd be good for.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want my son to have work.
portrait: Chloe Chen is a 58-year-old water cart and grader operator at the zinc mine at Morrow's Crossing, the third generation of her family at the mine, with her son Josh now a fitter there too. She uses a button phone, won't touch computers and trusts her church and family more than government. She is calm on the plateau, anxious under steady change mostly for her son, and alarmed if AGI arrives in two years and both of them lose their jobs at once. With five years she plans to scrape to her pension and build up her husband's mower shop, and with ten she's uneasy only for her son and grandchildren.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her son would lose their jobs at the same mine at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: The mine keeping apprentices and older workers on as long as possible, and the local community sticking together; she wants work for her son, not a handout.
